node.label: Capitalism, divergence and industrialisation
node.date_label: Capitalism and Slavery 1944 · Dobb–Sweezy 1950 · Brenner debate 1976–85 · Wrigley 1988 · de Vries 1994 · The Great Divergence 2000 · Allen and The Enlightened Economy 2009 · Empire of Cotton 2014 · Hilt 2017 · Burnard and Riello 2020
node.description: A set of linked arguments about why capitalism, industrialisation and Western wealth arose where and when they did. Marxist historians disputed whether trade or class relations ended feudalism: Dobb answered Sweezy that trade worked 'to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts' (1950). Brenner's property-relations thesis (1976) opened a second round, in which Bois called his approach 'political Marxism' and Wood made it a programme. Economic historians slowed the British Industrial Revolution while reasserting 'an important discontinuity' (Crafts and Harley, 1992), and Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' it; explanations multiplied in Wrigley's escape from an 'organic economy', de Vries's 'industrious revolution', Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' and Allen's high wages and cheap energy. Wong challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm; Pomeranz acknowledged that method while giving greater weight to global conjunctures, ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; critics answered from property relations, knowledge, wages and the state. Williams's Capitalism and Slavery (1944) returned through Inikori, the Legacies of British Slave-ownership project and an American 'history of capitalism' whose economic-historian critics charged 'specious arguments' (Hilt, 2017). Readers join these debates themselves: Burnard and Riello set the new history of capitalism beside the Brenner debate and Pomeranz (2020).

node.scope_note: A Debate entry with five components, each with its own strands: the transition debate; the Brenner debate and political Marxism; explaining industrialisation; the Great Divergence; slavery and capitalism. It gathers exchanges; each author's own contribution stays on the field entries, whose related strands are not moved: marx/transition, economic/marxist, economic/household_demand, economic/wrigley_growth, economic/regional_divergence, economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute (the Huang–Pomeranz exchange), economic/slavery_productivity_exchange, economic/empire, global/comparison, global/reciprocal_comparison_resources, global/protoindustry_trade_limits, consumption/household_labor, technology/invention_adoption, demography/aggregate_population, dependency/worldsystems, atlantic/earlier and quant/slavery_debate. Existing person entries (Dobb, Hilton, Williams, Pomeranz, Huang, Hall) keep their own relations; the new person entries are Brenner and Wood. Readings are recorded per source, many through publisher excerpts, abstracts, Cambridge Core chapter openings or reviewers; unread books are given only as named readers report them. Quotations from another copy of The Brenner Debate (1985) were withdrawn before drafting. The 'California School' is a readers' label, attributed by Frank (2001) and Vries (2009) to Goldstone. Toynbee (1884) is a dated precursor, not a start. Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries, Wong, Allen and Beckert are roster rows here; person entries for them are a later step.

strands.title: The transition debate: Dobb, Sweezy and their readers, 1946–1976
strands.focus: Dobb's Studies (1946) defined feudalism by the coercive relation between producer and lord; Sweezy (1950) answered that feudalism was 'a system of production for use' dissolved by 'causes external to the system', above all trade, while granting that 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Dobb replied that trade 'exercised its influence to the extent that it accentuated the internal conflicts', and carried the argument to the absolutist state and the English Revolution. Takahashi (1952) developed an analysis of production relations and the social form of labour, and pressed for fuller French and German comparison. Hilton collected the exchange with later essays in 1976. Positions within one Marxist debate, not a school. The field strands marx/transition and economic/marxist keep each author's own contribution.
strands.works: Dobb, Studies in the Development of Capitalism (1946); Sweezy and Dobb, Science & Society 14:2 (1950): 134–167; Takahashi (1952); Merrington, 'Town and Country in the Transition to Capitalism' (NLR, 1975); Hilton (ed.), The Transition from Feudalism to Capitalism (1976); see marx/transition and economic/marxist

strands.title: Against 'neo-Smithian Marxism': Brenner on Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein, 1977
strands.focus: Brenner traced Wallerstein's world-system and Frank's development of underdevelopment back to Sweezy's side of the 1950 debate and, through it, to 'the model put forward by Adam Smith'. He acknowledged a 'great debt' to Dobb, and credited Frank with breaking 'the suffocating orthodoxies' of stage theory. Callinicos (1990) called the critique 'a valuable corrective'. See dependency/worldsystems for Wallerstein's own account.
strands.works: Brenner, NLR I/104 (1977); Wallerstein, The Modern World-System I (1974); Frank (1966–)

strands.title: The Brenner debate in Past and Present, 1976–1985
strands.focus: Brenner argued that class structure decides how demographic and commercial change affects growth. Postan and Hatcher called his charges against them 'groundless'; Le Roy Ladurie defended a 'neo-Malthusian' model; Croot and Parker, Wunder and Klíma tested his English, French, German and Bohemian comparisons; Bois agreed against 'the Malthusian model' but not with Brenner's method. Brenner's reply (1982) spoke of 'social-property systems'. Hilton introduced the collection (1985) as 'a continuation' of the transition debate. The respondents are read only in their Cambridge Core openings; their later pages are unread, and Bois's specified later passages (pp. 115–116) are known only as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990); see annales/serial for Le Roy Ladurie's Languedoc.
strands.works: Past and Present 70 (1976) to 97 (1982); Aston and Philpin (eds), The Brenner Debate (1985)

strands.title: Political Marxism: from Bois's charge to a school, 1978–2016
strands.focus: Bois called Brenner's approach 'political Marxism', 'a voluntarist vision of history' (1978, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos, 1990). By the accounts of Callinicos (1990) and Brenner (2016), Wood accepted the label while rejecting the charge of voluntarism. She argued that 'the economic' and 'the political' are differently joined in pre-capitalist and capitalist societies (1981), against G. A. Cohen's technological determinism. Critics answered that it was 'little more than a sociology of domination' (Callinicos) and that Brenner, taking up Dobb, narrowed class struggle to the countryside (Harman).
strands.works: Bois (1978); Wood, 'The Separation of the Economic and the Political in Capitalism' (NLR, 1981), Democracy Against Capitalism (1995); Harman (1989); Callinicos, 'The Limits of "Political Marxism"' (NLR, 1990); Harman and Brenner (2004, printed 2006); Brenner (2016) and Hirschkop (2016) on Wood

strands.title: The origin of capitalism and its critics, 1991–2004
strands.focus: Wood argued that England was 'the world's first capitalist society' (1991), siding with Thompson against the Nairn–Anderson theses. In 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001) she set the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' against the 'commercialization model'; The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), unread here, is known through its jacket and McAuley's quotations. McAuley (2001), drawing on Blaut, criticised 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' for treating colonialism as marginal; Wood replied that slave plantations mattered 'quite a while after the emergence of capitalism in the English countryside'. This exchange joins the strand to the slavery and divergence components.
strands.works: Wood, The Pristine Culture of Capitalism (1991), The Origin of Capitalism (1999; 2002), 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001), replies (2002); McAuley (2001)

strands.title: Revolution or gradual growth? The Industrial Revolution revised, 1884–1994
strands.focus: Toynbee's posthumous lectures (1884) defined the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations'. Crafts and Harley's output estimates slowed its pace while reasserting 'the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity' (1992); Berg and Hudson answered that growth accounting had 'mis-specified' the subject and left out women's and children's labour, regional specialisation and innovation (1990 working paper; 1992). De Vries (1994) read the revisionists as 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off"', not pulling down the pillars.
strands.works: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (1884); Crafts and Harley (1992); Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper; EHR 1992); de Vries (JEH 1994), pp. 249–251; see historicalecon/british_teaching

strands.title: Rural industry and industrious households, 1972–2016
strands.focus: Mendels (1972) treated market-oriented rural industry as 'a first phase which preceded and prepared modern industrialization proper', and later called it 'a plausible and interesting set of hypotheses' (1984); the Göttingen group (Kriedte, Medick, Schlumbohm, 1977) placed rural industry in 'the genesis of capitalism'. Coleman (1983) titled his critique 'a concept too many'. De Vries's 'industrious revolution' (1994; 2008), a term van Nederveen Meerkerk traces to Akira Hayami, made household labour and demand precede the Industrial Revolution; reviewers asked whether consumption had become 'a new deus ex machina' (2009). Rosenband (2016), from French and English papermaking, challenged the model: paperworkers 'already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness', and women and adolescents worked for wages long before it (abstract). See economic/household_demand, consumption/household_labor and global/protoindustry_trade_limits for the field contributions.
strands.works: Mendels (JEH 1972) and NYRB letter (1984); Kriedte, Medick and Schlumbohm (1977; English 1981); Medick (1976); Coleman (1983); de Vries (1994; 2008); van Nederveen Meerkerk (2009); Rosenband (2016)

strands.title: Why Britain? Energy, knowledge and wages, 1988–2023
strands.focus: Wrigley (1988) questioned the Industrial Revolution as 'a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' and contrasted an 'organic economy' bounded by land with a mineral-based energy regime. Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment' was 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley doubted whether it described 'successful change at least as much as its cause' (2010). Allen (2009) argued that 'Wages were remarkably high, and energy was remarkably cheap', so 'it paid to invent it there'; Humphries charged the high-wage account with a 'patriarchal perspective' (2013), and Allen replied with evidence 'that women and children participated in the high wage economy' (2015, abstract). Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda found that, across English counties, industrialisation occurred where wages began low and mechanical skills high (2023, abstract); the result concerns differences within England, not Britain's international wage advantage, and the abstract does not name Allen. Clark and Jacks's coal-rent estimates imply a negligible income contribution from England's possession of coal reserves (2007). See economic/wrigley_growth and technology/invention_adoption.
strands.works: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988), The Path to Sustained Growth (2016); Mokyr (2002 paper), The Enlightened Economy (2009); Harley (2010); Allen (2009; 2015); Humphries (2013); Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2014; 2023); Clark and Jacks (2007)

strands.title: The Great Divergence and the so-called California School, 1997–2021
strands.focus: Wong (1997) challenged Europe's status as the comparative norm. Pomeranz (2000) followed 'a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed' while giving 'greater stress than Wong does on global conjunctures', and greater weight to ecological constraints, coal and New World resources; he dated divergence late. Readers attribute the label 'California School' to Goldstone (Frank 2001; Vries 2009), whose 'efflorescences' (2002) put pre-modern growth outside Europe too while locating the modern breakthrough in British engines, science and craft culture. Frank's ReOrient (1998) and a debate with Landes scheduled for December 1998, announced in a notice written from Frank's side, marked the polemical poles. Parthasarathi carried the argument to India (2011). Rosenthal and Wong, as Ma's review reports, explained divergence by political scale and war (2011); Ma found the hypothesis 'supported by fairly meager evidence'. Critics answered from property relations (Brenner and Isett 2002), knowledge (Mokyr 2002, 2012), wages and national accounts (Broadberry and Gupta 2006; Allen et al. 2011; Broadberry, Guan and Li 2021) and the state (Vries 2009, 2013). The Huang–Pomeranz exchange stays in economic/divergence_household_dispute and economic/coal_constraints_dispute.
strands.works: Wong, China Transformed (1997); Frank, ReOrient (1998); Landes, The Wealth and Poverty of Nations (1998); Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Frank's review (2001); Goldstone (2002); Brenner and Isett (2002); Mokyr (2002; 2012); Broadberry and Gupta (2006); Vries (2009; 2013); Parthasarathi (2011); Rosenthal and Wong (2011); Allen et al. (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li (2021); see global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources

strands.title: Capitalism and Slavery and its critics: the Williams thesis, 1944–2020
strands.focus: Williams (1944) advanced distinct propositions, which readers keep apart: that slave-trade and plantation wealth financed and stimulated British industry; that slave-derived wealth mattered in eighteenth-century Britain; and that the West Indies' economic decline, with changing economic interests, explains abolition. Drescher's Econocide (1977), in its publisher's description, challenged decline-based explanations of the 1807 abolition and stressed public mobilisation; Solow and Engerman's volume (1987) sifted the 'legacy'. Solow judged that slavery 'did not cause the Industrial Revolution but played an active role in its pattern and timing' (as quoted by Burnard and Riello), while Eltis and Engerman (2000), as Hilt and Burnard and Riello report them, judged its growth linkages to British industry small. Inikori (2002), as O'Rourke reports, reasserted the thesis through Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers. Hall (2014) and Burnard and Riello (2020) identify modified Williams arguments in Pomeranz and Inikori. The Legacies of British Slave-ownership team investigates slave-ownership's British legacies; its compensation evidence supports some Williams propositions, on slave-derived wealth, and qualifies the decline thesis, while leaving the industrialisation controversy unresolved ('Our material cannot resolve these controversies'). See economic/empire and atlantic/earlier.
strands.works: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery (1944); Drescher, Econocide (1977) and 'Capitalism and Slavery after Fifty Years' (1997); Solow and Engerman (eds), British Capitalism and Caribbean Slavery (1987); Eltis and Engerman (JEH 2000); Inikori, Africans and the Industrial Revolution in England (2002); Hall et al., Legacies of British Slave-ownership (2014)

strands.title: Slavery's capitalism and its economic-historian critics, 2013–2020
strands.focus: This strand selects the slavery controversy within the broader history of capitalism, a field whose early definition by Beckert, Hilt notes, is so broad that it 'includes most of the fields of labor, political, social, and business history', and whose work, Regele notes, began before the 2007–2009 financial crisis. Mainly Americanist historians, publicised as historians of capitalism in 2013, put slavery at the centre of American and global capitalism: Johnson's River of Dark Dreams (2013; Johnson does not count himself a historian of capitalism, Hilt notes), Baptist's argument, in Hilt's account, that torture drove cotton productivity (2014), Beckert's 'war capitalism' (2014) and Beckert and Rockman's Slavery's Capitalism (2016). Olmstead and Rhode answered that the books 'make fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (2017); Hilt, that 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine' them as social criticism, while granting that economic research supports some of their arguments and calling for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (2017); Burnard and Riello, that US cotton came 'too late to cause an Industrial Revolution' (2020). Readers trace the movement to Polanyi, the 2008 crisis and a turn from labour history (Hilt; Regele) and to Williams and Pomeranz (Burnard and Riello). Fogel and Engerman's earlier slavery debate stays in quant/slavery_debate.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Dobb–Sweezy transition debate (1950–76) as the first component of the debate on capitalism’s origins
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Science & Society 14:2 (1950), read in full: Sweezy's 'root cause … was the growth of trade' (p. 142) against Dobb's 'interaction of the two; although with primary emphasis … upon the internal contradictions' (p. 160). Readers who place it at the head of the line: Hilton (1978, p. 119; 1985, p. 1; Cambridge Core openings); Wood (2001, read): 'the famous Transition Debate which began in 1950 in Science and Society'; Harman (2004 transcript, read): 'The first stage took place in the 1940s and 1950s'. The field strand marx/transition keeps the positions; this arrow records the debate's place in the group entry.

proposed_edges.relationship: Feudalism defined by coercive production relations, with trade acting through internal conflicts: the debate’s founding text and reply (1946–50)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Dobb's reply, pp. 158, 160–161, 163, 165 (read): a definition 'advisedly in terms of the relations of production'; trade 'accentuated the internal conflicts'; labour services lasted longest 'in the more advanced south-east'; the seventeenth-century 'ruling class was still feudal'. Sweezy (p. 142): 'no theory which fails to take into account the factors which Dobb stresses … can be regarded as correct'. Wood (2001) and Harman (1989) treat Dobb as the start of the line Brenner continued. Distinct from edge_319 (Dobb → marx) and edge_479 (Dobb → economic).

proposed_edges.relationship: Class structure and property relations as the key to divergent European paths: the Brenner debate (1976–85) and the critique of neo-Smithian Marxism (1977)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Brenner 1976 (whole article OCRed; p. 31 read closely): 'it is the structure of class relations, of class power, which will determine the manner and degree to which particular demographic and commercial changes will affect long-run trends … and not vice versa' (p. 31). NLR 1977 (read in transcription): Sweezy, Frank and Wallerstein share 'the model put forward by Adam Smith' (§II). The editors' preface (1985, p. vii, Cambridge Core): 'one of the most important historical debates of recent years'. Wood (2001): 'Robert Brenner built on the foundation created by these Marxist historians'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Neo-Malthusian, Marxist and regional critics answer Brenner: the demographic historians misrepresented, 'political Marxism', doubtful England–France and east–west contrasts, class struggle narrowed to the countryside (1978–2004)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents the specified interventions of Postan and Hatcher, Le Roy Ladurie, Bois, Croot and Parker and Wunder in Past and Present (1978), and of Harman (1989; 2004) and Callinicos (1990); it is not a verdict of the group entry, which includes Brenner and his supporters. Postan and Hatcher: 'Both imputations are groundless' (p. 64). Le Roy Ladurie: 'somewhat superficial but also extremely insular'; 'simplistic assimilation between power (political) and surplus value (economic)' (pp. 101–102). Croot and Parker: 'Both halves of this argument are suspect' (p. 79). Wunder: 'fallen victim to the Prussian myth' (p. 91). Bois: 'radically disagreeing with his methodological orientation' (p. 107); 'a voluntarist vision of history' (pp. 115–116, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos 1990). Seccombe (1983): a 'tendency to deny the explanatory power of demographic phenomena'. Harman (1989): 'a very narrow view of class struggle'. Concessions kept: Croot and Parker, 'welcome and effective'; Bois, 'courageously attacks the Malthusian model'; Cooper, 'I sympathize with him'; Callinicos, 'a valuable corrective' (p. 111). The 1978 openings are read on Cambridge Core (1985 reprint pages); later pages are not quoted directly; the specified Bois passages (pp. 115–116) are mediated, as quoted by Wikipedia and Callinicos (1990).

proposed_edges.relationship: Collects the transition debate (1976) and introduces the Brenner debate as its continuation (1985)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Introduction to The Brenner Debate, p. 1 (Cambridge Core): 'In some respects it might be regarded as a continuation of that other well-known debate … which had been sparked off by the criticism by the American economist Paul Sweezy of the analysis given by Maurice Dobb'. 'A Crisis of Feudalism' (1978, p. 119, opening) traces the Marxist view from Dobb through Science and Society to Bois. The 1976 collection is known from its bibliographic record; its introduction is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Political Marxism and the agrarian origin of capitalism: the transition debate and Brenner's 'market dependence' set against the commercialization model (1981–2002)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wood, 'Eurocentric Anti-Eurocentrism' (2001, read in full): the Transition Debate 'challenged the commercialization model' but 'still shared significant assumptions' with it; Brenner explained 'the emergence of what he calls "market dependence"'. Pristine Culture (1991, publisher extract): 'Britain - or rather England - was the world's first capitalist society'. Readers: Callinicos (1990), 'Wood's employment of his work to construct "political Marxism"' (p. 112); Hirschkop (2016). The Origin of Capitalism itself is unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Marxist and anti-Eurocentric critics: 'little more than a sociology of domination', colonialism made marginal, and England made the only site of capitalism (1990–2004)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Callinicos (1990), McAuley (2001, with Blaut as he reports him) and Harman (2004). Callinicos (1990, pp. 112–114, read): 'Wood's "political Marxism" is little more than a sociology of domination'. McAuley (2001, read): 'the Brenner-Wood thesis' treats colonialism, in Blaut's words as he reports them, as 'a marginal process'. Harman (2004 transcript, read): her position takes Brenner's 'to a point of caricature … It is not Bob's'. Wood's replies (2002, read) are kept: 'I don't even remotely recognize my argument, or Brenner's'.

proposed_edges.relationship: Toynbee's Lectures (1884) define the Industrial Revolution as 'the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations', the concept the later debate revises
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Toynbee, Lectures on the Industrial Revolution in England (posthumous, 1884), Saylor transcription without print pages, read by lecture: Lecture I describes 'England on the eve of the Industrial Revolution'; Lecture VIII: 'The essence of the industrial Revolution is the substitution of competition for the medieval regulations which had previously controlled the production and distribution of wealth'; 'The effects of the industrial Revolution prove that free competition may produce wealth without producing well-being.' A reader's warrant: de Vries (1994, p. 249) calls the Industrial Revolution 'By far the most important such monument in economic history'. No claim that Toynbee coined the term or founded the debate; the chain to the 1980s passes through Clapham and Cannadine, unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Economic historians' measurement and its critics: Crafts and Harley's slower British growth with 'an important discontinuity' reasserted (1992), against Berg and Hudson's case that growth accounting 'mis-specified' the Industrial Revolution (1990/1992)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Crafts and Harley (1992, abstract, read): 'insofar as any adjustment is required the effect is slightly to lower the estimated growth rate … The idea of the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity is reasserted.' Berg and Hudson, working paper (May 1990, read in part): 'the gradualist perspective has appeared to triumph … because of a growing preoccupation with growth accounting' (p. 1); 'N. F. R. Crafts and others may not be able to find the industrial revolution because, in addition to using problematic data, they have mis-specified their subject' (pp. 4–5); 'It is time to move on from the macro accounting framework' (pp. 38–39); 1992 abstract: 'Gradualist perspectives now dominate'. De Vries (1994, pp. 250–251, read) on Lindert and Williamson, Harley and Crafts: 'cleansing the temple of the "false god of the take off," not … pulling down the pillars'. 'Gradualist' is the critics' label; Crafts and Harley reassert a discontinuity.

proposed_edges.relationship: Population history in the industrialisation debate: Wrigley turns from population to the 'organic economy' (1988), and Berg and Hudson read Wrigley and Schofield's demographic continuity as 'aggregative' (1990)
proposed_edges.map_label: From population history to the organic economy, 1988–2016
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wrigley, Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, publisher excerpt): 'After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution' (p. 1); 'My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon' (p. 3); the classical economists' writings remain authoritative 'within the confines of … an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy' (p. 5); coal and steam 'entirely transformed' the prospects for growth (p. 6). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): 'Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.' Berg and Hudson (1990): 'The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.' Wrigley has no entry in this revision; the arrow is drawn from the field that holds his population work (demography/aggregate_population).

proposed_edges.relationship: Household demand as an explanation of industrialisation: de Vries's 'industrious revolution' answers the Crafts–Harley revision (1994) and is extended to 1650–1850 (2008); a reviewer asks whether consumption became a 'deus ex machina' (2009)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: De Vries (JEH 1994, pp. 249–251 read): 'The Industrial Revolution as a historical concept has many shortcomings. A new concept—the "industrious revolution"—is proposed to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting … a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon'; he frames it against the revision of 'Peter Lindert and Jeffrey Williamson, Knick Harley, and Nick Crafts' (pp. 250–251). Van Nederveen Meerkerk (TSEG 2009, read in full): Akira Hayami used the term earlier for Japan and 'De Vries adopteerde het begrip'; consumption becomes 'een nieuwe "deus ex machina"' (p. 176). Rosenband (2016, abstract): papermaking raises 'fundamental challenges to this model'. Pomeranz used the concept for Chinese households (2000, p. 17). The household mechanism itself stays on consumption/household_labor and economic/household_demand.

proposed_edges.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause: Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment', 'the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (2002 draft); reviewing The Enlightened Economy (2009), Harley found that it seemed to describe 'successful change at least as much as its cause' (2010)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mokyr, 'The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle' (author's draft, October 2002, read pp. 1–4, 10): Enlightenment thinkers 'created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention' (p. 10). Harley, EH.Net review of Mokyr's book The Enlightened Economy (2009), December 2010 (EH.Net original read, no pages; wording checked 2026-10-18): 'The reader cannot, however, help wondering if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed. The so-called Industrial Enlightenment seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.' The Industrial Enlightenment quotation is from the 2002 draft only; the 2009 book is unread and known here through Harley's review. Mokyr's earlier distinction of invention and adoption stays on technology/invention_adoption. Mokyr has no entry in this revision.

proposed_edges.relationship: Pomeranz's reassessment of divergence timing, 2011, as reported by Vries: he 'probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence', and parity had probably gone by 1750 'if not in 1700'
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Vries, Escaping Poverty (2013, p. 17, read), on Pomeranz's 'Ten Years After' (2011, unread): 'the most important Californian, Kenneth Pomeranz, very recently admitted that he probably overstated the lateness and suddenness of the Great Divergence and that economic parity between the two extremes of Eurasia probably had already disappeared in 1750 if not in 1700' (n. 23 cites de Vries's 'after ten years' and Pomeranz's 'Ten years after'). A contribution to the debate's chronology by its principal author, known through one reader's report; a concession, not a critique. Moderate. Pomeranz's 2002–2003 replies concern Huang and stay on edges 1043–1044.

proposed_edges.relationship: Reciprocal comparison as the California School's method: Wong (1997), Pomeranz (2000) and Parthasarathi's 'parallels in Eurasia' (2011), read by Vries as 'a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians' (2013)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pomeranz (2000, pp. 7–8, read): a regional approach 'anticipated in important ways by my colleague R. Bin Wong'; 'Here, too, I am following a procedure outlined in Wong's recent China Transformed … viewing both sides of the comparison as "deviations" when seen through the expectations of the other'. Parthasarathi (2011, publisher excerpt): earlier explanations 'all identify something that made Europe different … This book takes a different approach … it rejects claims for European difference' (p. 1); 'Kenneth Pomeranz builds upon this work' (p. 5). Vries (2013, pp. 14–15, read): 'The Californians, moreover, experiment with a new kind of comparative reciprocal history that suits global historians who not only want to juxtapose but also connect.' The method strands stay on global/comparison and global/reciprocal_comparison_resources.

proposed_edges.relationship: Frank's ReOrient (1998) as the polemical wing of the divergence debate: Asia central until 1800, a debate with Landes announced for December 1998 and an endorsement of Pomeranz (2001)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Notice announcing the Landes–Frank debate (Northeastern University, scheduled for 2 December 1998; read; written from Frank's side; whether the debate took place as announced is not independently confirmed): 'FRANK retorts that … Received social theory … is vitiated by the ingrained EUROCENTRISM of historiography'; Asia 'remained predominant in the world until at 1800'; 'LANDES retorts that Frank and his echoes are a magnet for fallacies and fantasies'. Frank's review of Pomeranz (JAS 2001; author's manuscript read): 'bar none, the biggest and most important contribution'; Pomeranz is 'the most important … member of what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'. Mokyr (EH.Net 2012, read): 'The California School, most notably embodied in Kenneth Pomeranz's Great Divergence and Andre Gunder Frank's Re-Orient'. Vries (2013, pp. 15–16) quotes ReOrient (pp. 75, 259) and calls one passage 'a quite silly statement'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 228 n.): Beckert 'is heavily influenced by [world-systems theory's] axioms'. ReOrient itself is unread. Distinct from edge_1053 (Pomeranz → dependency).

proposed_edges.relationship: Goldstone's 'efflorescences' of pre-modern growth (2002), and the 'California School' label that readers attribute to him
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Goldstone (JWH 2002, abstract): 'many premodern and non-Western economies show spurts or efflorescences of economic growth … Medieval Europe, Golden Age Holland, and Qing China'; the distinctive Western combination 'developed from the seventeenth to nineteenth centuries only in Britain'. The label: Frank (2001, read), 'what Jack Goldstone has called the new "California School"'; Vries (2009, p. 35 n. 1, read), 'The term was introduced by Jack Goldstone.' Goldstone's own first use was not found. Vries (2009, p. 48) adds that Californians should 'broaden their approach, as some, e.g. Jack Goldstone, have already done'. Goldstone's earlier comparative work stays on historicalsociology/demographic_crises.

proposed_edges.relationship: Capitalism and Slavery (1944) as the starting point of the slavery-and-capitalism component: four arguments taken up and modified by economic historians and by the new history of capitalism
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Readers, read: Burnard and Riello (JGH 2020, p. 227): 'Four of his arguments are critical to the NHC project: that slavery was central to the Industrial Revolution; that slave wealth was important to the history of eighteenth-century Britain; that the West Indian slave economy went into decline from 1783; and that West Indian slave-owners moved from being a progressive force within mercantilism to being a reactionary force within industrial capitalism'; 'His contemporary defenders, however, use Williams for historical perspectives he never considered' (p. 227); 'a movement among economic historians that accepts a modified version of the Williams thesis' (p. 233). Hilt (JEH 2017, p. 516): 'Like Eric Williams in Capitalism and Slavery (1944), Beckert argues …'; n. 6: Inikori (2002) is 'the strongest recent defense of the Williams hypothesis'. Regele (2023, p. 7): the new work draws on 'a long history of scholarship … most notably Eric Williams's Capitalism and Slavery'. Pomeranz (2000, p. 3 n. 2): 'the generally negative current mainstream verdicts on the arguments of Eric Williams (1944)'. Distinct from edge_155 (Williams → economic) and edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

proposed_edges.relationship: Atlantic trade and African producers and consumers in the making of the Industrial Revolution: Inikori's reassertion of Williams (2002), with the 1987 conference volume on Williams's legacy as its precedent
proposed_edges.evidence_note: O'Rourke, EH.Net review of Inikori (2003; read in part): 'His argument is that international trade was crucial to the success of that revolution, in particular trade with the Atlantic Basin (Africa, the West Indies, and the Americas); and that Africans on both sides of the Atlantic were central to this process, both as consumers and producers'; 'a lot of cliometricians will probably conclude that Inikori's argument is not as yet proven'. Burnard and Riello (2020, p. 227): Inikori is 'Williams' best modern-day defender', concerned that 'the Industrial Revolution owed much more to Africa and Africans than previously thought'. Solow and Engerman (eds, 1987): contents only, with chapters by Solow, Inikori, Richardson and Drescher. Inikori's book itself is unread. Distinct from edge_406 (Williams → atlantic).

proposed_edges.relationship: Economic historians answer the new history of capitalism: 'fundamental errors in economic reasoning' (Olmstead and Rhode, 2017) and 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning' that 'sometimes undermine' the books (Hilt, 2017); Olmstead and Rhode attribute the observed productivity increase primarily to biological innovation, as Hilt reports
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Olmstead and Rhode, AHA paper (programme abstract read; scheduled for 8 January 2017): 'The "New History of Capitalism" grounds the rise of industrial capitalism on the production of raw cotton by American slaves … We show that all make fundamental errors in economic reasoning that affect their major interpretations'; Baptist's torture argument 'is at variance with the ex-slave narratives that he cites and with evidence drawn from plantation records'. Hilt (JEH 2017, read pp. 511–520): 'specious arguments and failures of analytical reasoning sometimes undermine these books' effectiveness as social criticism' (p. 511); 'None of the books makes any attempt to falsify major elements of their arguments' (p. 515); on Baptist, Olmstead and Rhode 'show that the increase in productivity they observe was due primarily to biological innovations' (p. 518). Qualification: economic-historical research 'casts doubt on some of these arguments and lends support to others' (p. 516), and Hilt calls for 'dialogue, if not collaboration' (p. 511). Hilt reports a measured productivity increase explained primarily by biological innovation; this is not a claim that coercion was absent. The 2018 article is known from metadata only. The earlier Fogel–Engerman debate stays on quant/slavery_debate.
